# Building a strength training program

Parameters in descending order of importance: volume → frequency → proximity to failure → rep range → exercise order → exercise selection. Don't obsess over the lower levels until the upper ones are dialed in.

## 1. Volume — the main parameter

- Volume = **working sets per muscle group per week**. A working set: warmed up, target weight, 1–5 (avg ~3) reps in reserve.
- Reference points: ~6 sets/week is the edge of effective (already grows a beginner); **10 / 15 / 20** are the working numbers; 25+ only for the experienced under supervision; 50 is overkill.
- The growth mechanism is **mechanical tension** in near-failure sets at 30–80% 1RM. Muscle damage does NOT drive growth ("microtears → growth" is a myth).
- Each set = stimulus + cost (systemic and local fatigue). Overtraining = cost > stimulus. The optimum is individual and shifts: stress, sleep, nutrition, and dieting lower the ceiling → adjust volume down.
- Honest tradeoff for the busy: ~10 sets/week = slower but cheap in time and recovery; 20 = more growth, more expensive.
- Excess volume is insidious — it may not be felt at all. It's caught only by logging: if you grow the same or better on less volume — cut volume.
- To **maintain** muscle you need ~3× less work than to progress (enough during cuts and travel).

## 2. Frequency

- **≥2×/week per group**: elevated protein synthesis after training lasts at most ~72 hours. 1×/week = the muscle grows half the week.
- Ceiling of productive work **per session: ~8–10 sets per group** (different patterns for one group — up to ~15). Beyond that is wasted.
- Large volume → split it up: 25 sets/week = at least 3 sessions. Small endurance-y groups (delts) can be trained up to 5×/week in mini-doses.
- Default week structure: **beginner — full-body 2–3×/week; beyond that — upper/lower 4×/week or full-body more often**. The bro-split is suboptimal (but robust to mistakes — "idiot-proofing").

## 3. Proximity to failure (RIR)

- Default: **2–3 in reserve**. 0–1 is acceptable on isolation with good technique; 4–5 is too far.
- **Compounds — with reserve, isolation — closer to/into failure** (the stimulus there is cheaper and safer).
- People systematically overestimate proximity to failure by 10–20 reps (legs especially). Periodically **calibrate**: take it to true failure in a safe exercise (leg press with safety stops).
- Adjust to psychotype: loves grinding → allow failure but cut volume; loves to chill → more volume at RIR 3–4.

## 4. Rep range and load

- **5–30 reps near failure grow muscle equally** (solid consensus). Above ~30 it shifts toward endurance. Low reps cost more in recovery.
- Cover each group with different ranges; the proportions follow user preference.
- Women: higher endurance below 90% 1RM — fine, as long as they do more reps at the same %.

## 5. Exercise order

- Whatever's first gets done best (fresh nervous system). The priority/lagging group goes first.
- Coordination-heavy work (Olympic lifts) — only at the start.
- Default: a big compound first (rows/pull-ups), another compound second, then isolation.

## 6. Exercise selection

- Algorithm: tier lists from evidence-based authors (Jeff Nippard) → understand the criteria → try them on yourself → keep the ones that work for you personally.
- Criteria of a good exercise: you can do ~5 sets without "dying"; full safe range of motion; **load in the stretched position of the muscle** (in the shortened position the stimulus doesn't matter — which is why bands alone make growth hard). Trend: lengthened partials — partial reps in the stretched position.
- **SFR (stimulus-to-fatigue ratio)** is the main personalization filter: stimulus (pump, feeling the target muscle work, progression) vs cost (fatigue, joints, weird sensations). Joint pain — the exercise is dropped immediately. SFR is dynamic — an exercise can "get more expensive" months later.
- The classic deadlift is a poor hypertrophy exercise (small joint angles for every muscle); **the Romanian deadlift is more advantageous** for the posterior chain. The lifter's deadlift and squat can be skipped entirely if the goal is body composition.
- For a group with many functions (glutes) — a **diversified portfolio of patterns**: squat pattern (low-bar version) + bridge/hip thrust + hip hinge (Romanian, good morning) + 2–3 isolation movements at different angles. Science doesn't know "the best" — cover all functions.
- The back isn't one group: spinal erectors / lats (vertical AND horizontal pulls separately) / mid-upper back / rear delts. "The deadlift trains the whole back" is a myth (only the erectors, dynamically).

## 7. Machines vs free weights, gym vs home

- For hypertrophy they're **equal**. Skill transfer is one-way: free weight → machine. Beginners should set technique with free weights.
- Machines: risk of overuse injuries from a fixed path → **rotate every few months**.
- Progress at home is perfectly possible; the gym is only better for its selection of tools (higher chance of finding an exercise with good SFR). The weak spot at home is the hamstrings.
- Home equipment by priority: pull-up bar → bands (+BFR cuffs — a methodology that works) → adjustable dumbbells → TRX → incline bench → push-up handles.
- The main risk at home is a progression dead-end: exercise modifications (feet elevated, bands, handles) exist precisely to restore progression.

## 8. Progression and plateaus

- The program must allow adding **+1–2 reps or minimal weight every 1–2 weeks**. By weight or by reps — doesn't matter.
- "Surprising the muscle" isn't needed — variety for variety's sake doesn't work.
- **3–4 weeks without progression = stagnation** → swap the exercise for an analog of the same pattern, progress for 2–3 months, then you can come back (good odds of breaking the old plateau).
- Strength gains are mostly skill (neural adaptation), not +X% muscle. Don't interpret a beginner's fast weight gains as muscle gain.

## 9. Recovery and signs of overreaching

- You can't "fry your CNS" with bodybuilding; what's real is neuromuscular fatigue: if your weights collapse by the end of the session, the stimulus of the next sets ≈ 0 — finish up.
- Signs of overreaching: strange sharp muscle pain (≠ DOMS) → finish with that group, possibly drop it for ~2 weeks; **joint pain → stop the exercise immediately**; leaving the gym "wrecked for 2–3 hours" → overreaching (correct is leaving refreshed). Between "refreshed" and "wrecked" is ~2 sets — that's how you calibrate your personal per-session ceiling.
- Little sleep / stress / deficit → lower effective volume → adjust the plan down.
- Alcohol: −testosterone ~1–2 days (men), −strength ~2 days, calories from snacks go to fat. Rare exceptions don't show long-term.

## 10. Cardio + lifting

- Interference effect: large volumes of aerobic and strength work conflict. **Separate days**; if impossible — different times of day + a large carb intake between. Antipattern: an hour of barbell → 40 min on the treadmill.
- 15 min of easy walking after lifting is harmless. For health, ~10,000 steps/day is enough; endurance trains only specifically ("want a gas tank — train the gas tank").

## 11. Mobility and stretching

- Working through a full range of motion with emphasis on stretched positions develops mobility on its own (as effectively as stretching). Exception — the thoracic spine/upper back: needs separate work.
- **Static stretching before lifting — no** (acutely reduces strength); dynamic only. After — fine, no proven benefit. Stretching for DOMS — unconfirmed.

## 12. Goals, motivation, expectations

- Goals — as **rate-of-change over time** ("+1 rep/week"), not absolutes ("bench 150"). The potential is unknown in advance.
- Feedback loops: reps — within a week; weights — 2–3 weeks; the mirror — 3–6 months. Metrics (logs, girths, caliper folds) are needed to see progress before the mirror does.
- Dopamine in the process: favorite exercises, rituals, the state after training. Enjoyment = consistency = results.
- For a beginner: train everything (no prioritization needed), technique with free weights, ideally an in-person coach with a specific request "set my technique on the main patterns" (empty bar, from day one — squat, pulls, presses, without "a million prep exercises").
- Coach red flags: everything to failure; PEDs for a beginner; "sacrifice everything"; rigid "only this way"; isolation instead of teaching the basic patterns.
